name: Nora Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run my own piano studio in a rented room above a bakery on Mill Street. I've got about thirty-five students, from six-year-olds to a retired judge, plus a handful I teach online. Friday and Saturday nights I play the piano bar at the Alder Hotel, which is standards, film songs and whatever the wedding guests request after their third drink.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you run the business side?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly with AI, honestly. I use it every day for scheduling, invoices, reminder messages to parents, and to write custom practice pieces for each student at their exact level. Running thirty-five students used to eat every Sunday, and now the admin takes me forty minutes. That freed up time I put into more teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a nice assistant, not a teacher, which is what I already say. I'd probably mention it to parents who ask whether their kids still need lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wouldn't change anything for me. I already use the routine stuff. My students come for a person who notices their wrist is tense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and probably expand. There's a waiting list of eight kids, so I'd look at renting a second room and hiring another teacher two days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's stopped you hiring already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly finding the right person. My friend Leila from college might do it if the hours suited her. A waiting list of eight children is the best problem a piano teacher can have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything outside AI that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent above the bakery went up this year, and the landlord hints it'll go up again. That's the thing I actually lose sleep over, a little.

steps.text: Keep teaching thirty-five students and Friday and Saturday hotel nights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say teachers who use the tools will do better than those who don't. I'd post about how I use them, because a lot of teachers I know are scared and don't need to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. My admin gets even smaller, my practice materials get better, and parents still want a person in the room. Some cheaper online teaching will go to apps, but that's a small part of my income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the studio and offer group classes for young kids, which are hands-on and fun. I'd build a little AI practice companion for my students to use between lessons, with my own exercises. I'd keep the hotel nights because they're easy money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the online students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those five or six would probably drift to apps, and I'd let them. I'd lose the online students to apps and gain them back as children in a room on Saturday mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Older teachers who don't use any of this. Mrs Brandt, my old teacher, is seventy and still invoices by hand. She'd be fine with her loyal families, but newer teachers who copy her would struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than anyone can manage and we need sensible support for people losing jobs. I'd keep telling parents music is still worth learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two things. Parents losing their own jobs will cut piano lessons first, because lessons are a treat. And robots around 2031 could teach technique, maybe not well, but cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the second room and keep the cash. I'd move towards group classes, which are cheaper per family and harder to replace. I'd talk to Sam about whether we'd be fine on his physio income if mine dropped by half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My students' parents are the ones who'd get hit, and that comes straight back to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think your students would actually quit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. I've seen it before, when a parent loses their job. Piano lessons are the first thing a family cancels and the last thing they add back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Sam's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Physiotherapy is hands-on, so he'd have until robots, at least. I think he'd be okay longer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people are smart. I'd keep showing teachers how I use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years means I can grow first and then adjust. Parents' jobs start going around 2031, robots around 2034. That's time to build a solid group-class business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hire Leila and open the second room now, but on a short lease. I'd build the group programme quickly. I'd save more from the hotel nights so there's a bigger cushion before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see a way to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a short lease?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So I can get out if things turn. A two-year lease on a second room is a bet I can walk away from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the hotel work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Hotel guests want a person playing, and it's easy. I'd keep it as long as they'll have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and teachers should start learning the tools now so they aren't caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means my studio could be properly established, maybe two or three teachers. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with kids of my own. Plenty of time to adjust when robots come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expand fully: second room, two teachers, group classes. I'd automate all the admin and build better practice tools. And I'd keep an eye on things each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about selling the studio some day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, around 2035, to one of my teachers. Selling the studio to one of my own teachers in ten years would feel like a good ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would change that calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, again. If the bakery building gets sold, I'd have to move everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because parents' jobs would go before I could adjust. What would help is support for families so kids can keep their lessons, and maybe a rent cap for small studios like mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about rent. Every small music business I know worries more about rent than about AI.
